content: Etodolac is a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) that may increase the risk of heart attack or stroke, especially in individuals who take it for a prolonged period. These cardiovascular events can occur without warning and may be fatal. Inform your doctor if you or your family have a history of heart disease, heart attack, or stroke, if you smoke, or if you have high cholesterol, high blood pressure, or diabetes. Seek emergency medical attention immediately if you experience chest pain, shortness of breath, weakness on one side of the body, or slurred speech. Do not take etodolac before or after coronary artery bypass graft (CABG) surgery. Etodolac and other NSAIDs can cause ulcers, bleeding, or perforations in the stomach or intestines, which may occur at any time during treatment, often without warning symptoms, and can be life-threatening. The risk is higher for individuals who take NSAIDs long-term, are older, are in poor health, or consume large amounts of alcohol. Inform your doctor if you are taking anticoagulants (e.g., warfarin), aspirin, other NSAIDs (e.g., ibuprofen, naproxen), or oral steroids (e.g., prednisone). Also, let your doctor know if you have a history of stomach or intestinal ulcers, bleeding disorders, or other bleeding issues. Stop taking etodolac and contact your doctor if you experience stomach pain, heartburn, vomiting blood or material resembling coffee grounds, blood in the stool, or black, tarry stools. Keep all appointments with your doctor and laboratory for monitoring. Your doctor will carefully assess your symptoms and may order tests to evaluate your response to etodolac. Always communicate how you are feeling so your doctor can adjust your medication to minimize the risk of serious side effects. You will receive a Medication Guide from your doctor or pharmacist when starting etodolac and with each prescription refill. Read it carefully and ask any questions you may have. Etodolac is prescribed to relieve pain, tenderness, swelling, and stiffness caused by osteoarthritis and rheumatoid arthritis. It is also used to manage pain from other causes. Etodolac works by inhibiting the production of substances in the body that cause pain, fever, and inflammation. Etodolac is available as tablets, capsules, and extended-release tablets for oral use. For arthritis, tablets and capsules are typically taken two to three times daily, while extended-release tablets are taken once daily. For other types of pain, tablets and capsules are usually taken every 6 to 8 hours. Take etodolac at the same time(s) each day, following your doctor’s instructions exactly. Do not take more or less than prescribed. Swallow extended-release tablets whole; do not split, chew, or crush them. If you are taking etodolac for arthritis, your doctor may start you on a higher dose and reduce it once your symptoms are controlled. It may take 1–2 weeks to feel the full benefits of this medication. Before taking etodolac, inform your doctor if you are allergic to it, aspirin, other NSAIDs, or any of its inactive ingredients. Provide a list of all prescription and nonprescription medications, vitamins, and supplements you are taking, especially those mentioned in the Important Warning section. Mention if you have asthma, nasal polyps, swelling in the extremities, or kidney or liver disease. If you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding, inform your doctor. If you become pregnant while taking etodolac, contact your doctor immediately. Inform your healthcare provider if you are undergoing surgery, including dental procedures. Unless directed otherwise by your doctor, continue your normal diet while taking etodolac. If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. If it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and continue your regular schedule. Do not take a double dose to make up for a missed one. Etodolac may cause minor side effects such as constipation, diarrhea, gas, bloating, vomiting, headache, dizziness, ringing in the ears, runny nose, sore throat, or blurred vision. Inform your doctor if these symptoms persist or worsen. Serious side effects include unexplained weight gain, swelling of the face or extremities, fever, chills, blisters, rash, itching, hives, hoarseness, difficulty breathing or swallowing, yellowing of the skin or eyes, extreme fatigue, unusual bleeding or bruising, loss of appetite, upper right abdominal pain, flu-like symptoms, pale skin, rapid heartbeat, cloudy or bloody urine, painful urination, or back pain. Stop taking etodolac and contact your doctor immediately if you experience any of these symptoms. Store etodolac in its original container, tightly closed, and out of reach of children. Keep it at room temperature, away from excess heat and moisture. Do not store it in the bathroom. Dispose of expired or unneeded medication properly by consulting your pharmacist. In case of overdose, contact a poison control center at 1-800-222-1222 or call 911 if the individual collapses or is not breathing. Symptoms of overdose may include extreme fatigue, drowsiness, upset stomach, vomiting, stomach pain, bloody or black stools, vomit resembling coffee grounds, or loss of consciousness. Before undergoing any laboratory tests, inform your doctor and lab personnel that you are taking etodolac. If you have diabetes and test your urine for ketones, be aware that etodolac may interfere with test results. Consult your doctor about monitoring your diabetes while on this medication. Do not share your medication with others. If you have questions about refilling your prescription, ask your pharmacist.
